kurz: How to determine monthly income, monthly expenditure and net worth on a reference date, and what these three figures say about your household.

bloecke.md:
Almost everyone knows their gross salary. Far fewer people can say how much money left their account last year, and fewer still what they own after deducting their debts. The reason lies in the payment infrastructure rather than in any flaw of character. Direct debits, card payments and subscriptions spread spending across the month in such small pieces that a total never appears anywhere.

Three figures are enough for an overview, and they belong to two different concepts of time. Income and expenditure are [[Flow variable|flow variables]]: they apply to a period. [[Net worth]] is a stock variable and applies to a reference date. Mixing the two, for example by comparing a portfolio value of €20,000 with a monthly savings amount of €300, produces comparisons that seem plausible but say nothing.

Net income and expenditure are recorded per month, net worth on a reference date. The difference between the flows is the savings amount; the change in the stock is the result. The two only match if neither price movements nor loan repayments come into play.

## Roles of the current account, instant-access savings and the securities account

The current account is for making payments, not for keeping money. Money that sits there for longer than a month has no assigned purpose. It looks like a reserve and still gets spent, because the balance shows it as available.

An instant-access savings account visibly separates the savings buffer. The balance is available every day, and a transfer to the current account takes up to two bank working days. Up to €100,000 per customer and bank, instant-access savings are covered by statutory [[deposit protection]]. The interest rate follows the ECB deposit facility rate, which stood at 2.50% on 16 September 2026. Higher promotional rates usually apply only to new customers and only for a few months. The next lesson covers how large the savings buffer should be. Money with an investment horizon of ten years or more belongs in the securities account.

The order of the bookings within the month matters more than the number of accounts. A standing order on the day after your salary arrives turns the savings amount into a fixed item, just like the fixed costs. If you only save what is left at the end of the month, no savings build up in the long run. An automatic transfer is therefore more reliable than discipline.

bloecke.titel: Account model with a fixed order of transfers
bloecke.unter: The savings amount is debited before any spending, so the spending account shows what is still available to spend without any further calculation.

bloecke.md:
## Methods for recording expenditure

There are three methods for the spending side, and they differ mainly in the effort involved.

The classic **household budget book** records every payment. It is the only method that also captures cash payments, and the act of writing things down already influences spending behaviour. In return, it has to be kept up continuously, and three months are not enough for an evaluation, because insurance premiums, vehicle tax, holidays, repairs and Christmas do not fall in every quarter.

**Bank statement analysis** works retrospectively. Twelve months of transactions are exported as a CSV file, sorted by payee and grouped into categories. This takes one evening instead of a year and captures all annual items. One gap remains with cash, which only shows up as individual withdrawals.

The **difference method** needs no categories. You note the total of all account balances and portfolio values on 1 January and on 31 December and adjust for the change in prices. This gives you the year's savings, and expenditure is then net income minus savings. The method is accurate but does not show what the money was spent on. It makes sense to categorise thoroughly once and after that only check the difference.

bloecke.md:
## Fixed costs and regular costs

[[Fixed costs]] are the costs you cannot change in the short term. Arising every month does not make a cost fixed. What counts is the time until a change is possible. For a flat it is three months, for a mobile phone contract it is the end of the term, and the broadcasting fee cannot be changed at all. Groceries also arise every month but can be influenced from tomorrow.

Annual payments are divided by twelve. Otherwise the budget shows a surplus for eleven months and does not add up in the twelfth. Cuts to fixed costs work through repetition. An item reduced once saves money twelve times a year without any further decision. Variable costs, by contrast, require you to go without afresh each time.

The model household switches its mobile tariff (€60 → €25) and its electricity supplier (€55 → €43) and cancels an unused subscription (€30). This saves €77 a month and €924 a year.

Relative to annual net income of €31,200, the savings rate rises by 2.96 percentage points from 17.7% to 20.7%, without a single everyday spending decision. Achieving the same effect through variable costs requires spending around €80 less per month and twelve new decisions a year.

bloecke.formel: Savings rate = (Net income − Expenditure) / Net income × 100
bloecke.erklaerung: The savings rate is always based on net income, never on gross income, and always calculated over twelve months, because monthly figures fluctuate too much.
variablen: everything that actually comes in: pay after tax and social security contributions, child benefit (Kindergeld), side income, refunds
all outflows except what goes into your own assets

bloecke.md:
## Defining the savings rate

There is no uniform definition for calculating the [[savings rate]]. This has practical consequences, because depending on the definition the result can double.

The narrow version counts only what flows into your own accounts or into the portfolio. The broad version adds the repayment of a mortgage loan, which is economically correct because repayment builds net worth and interest does not. Some versions also include contributions to an occupational pension (betriebliche Altersvorsorge). The most disputed item is the compulsory contributions to the statutory pension insurance. The employee's share of 9.3% builds entitlements, but no capital that you could draw on or leave to your heirs.

The economy-wide savings rate from the national accounts (Volkswirtschaftliche Gesamtrechnung) is not suitable as a personal benchmark either. It is defined differently and contains items that never appear in any private account. Only your own figure is useful, and only if it is carried forward over several years according to a rule fixed at the outset.

bloecke.titel: The 50/30/20 rule and two households with the same net income
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the same net income, the same consumption and a rent difference of only €350; the deviation from the rule is due to rent alone.

bloecke.md:
## The 50/30/20 rule and its limits

The split into 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% saving and debt repayment comes from the American guide *All Your Worth* by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi. It can be checked in a minute but has structural limits. First, it refers to a net income that is arrived at differently in the United States. German net pay already has around 21% in social security contributions deducted, including contributions to health, long-term care and pension insurance. In the United States, contributions to the state pension (Social Security) are also deducted before net pay, but the rule counts health insurance premiums as needs. Second, the 50% threshold is out of reach for many renting households in German metropolitan areas. As the chart shows, the same person with the same spending behaviour ends up at 65% or at 51.5% depending on where they live. Third, the rule lumps saving and paying off debt together, although repaying an arranged overdraft at around 11.5% and paying into a savings plan differ in urgency.

As a diagnostic tool the rule remains useful, because the deviation shows which of the three quantities shapes the structure. Understood as a fixed prescription, it only leads to a sense of failure.

If the savings rate is too low, hunting for ten euros of savings does little. It is more useful to check which of the three quantities can be changed at all. Rent, transport and income account for most of the range. A move or a salary negotiation changes the savings rate to an extent that no everyday sacrifice can match, and it requires a one-off effort instead of daily self-control.

bloecke.formel: Net worth = Total assets − Total liabilities
bloecke.erklaerung: Net worth is calculated on a reference date. What counts is what could be realised today, not what was once paid in or will fall due later.

bloecke.md:
## Valuation in the personal balance sheet

On the asset side, three valuation decisions have to be made, and mistakes are common with all of them. An endowment policy goes on the balance sheet at its [[surrender value]], not at the premiums paid in and not at the projected maturity benefit. In the first years this value is often well below the amount paid in, because acquisition costs of up to 2.5% of total premiums are offset up front. A property is entered at a cautiously estimated market value, not at the purchase price. A car loses value as a matter of course. If it is carried at its price when new, the balance sheet shows wealth that is in the process of disappearing. Household contents are usually not included.

The liability side includes everything that is legally owed, that is, outstanding loan balances, overdrawn balances, assessed additional tax payments and unpaid bills. Future rent or subscription fees do not belong there, because they are matched by use and can be cancelled.

The balance sheet is drawn up once a year on the same reference date. Its change is what tells you the most, because it combines the savings amount, repayments and price movements. The savings rate, by contrast, only measures what you can control yourself. Both figures are needed and should not be offset against each other.

bloecke.titel: Pension entitlement outside the balance sheet
bloecke.md:
For many households, the statutory pension is the largest item in their retirement provision, yet it appears in no statement of wealth. This follows from the valuation rule. The pension entitlement cannot be sold or borrowed against and can only be inherited to a limited extent, so it has no realisable value on the reference date.

You should still know its order of magnitude. From 1 July 2026, one earnings point (Entgeltpunkt) corresponds to a monthly gross pension of €42.52. The standard pension from 45 earnings points is €1,913.40 gross. With 25 earnings points there is an entitlement of just over €1,060 a month, which appears in the balance sheet as zero. The overview should therefore include a second, separate line that records the figure from the annual pension statement (Renteninformation) alongside net worth.

bloecke.titel: Net worth per household in Germany
bloecke.unter: Means from the 2023 income and consumption survey (Einkommens- und Verbrauchsstichprobe), median from the wealth survey of the same years; because the figures come from two surveys, they only show the order of magnitude.

bloecke.md: The average of €230,400 does not describe a typical household. Wealth in Germany is very unevenly distributed, and the median is around €103,200, so half of all households have less. Salaries show the same effect. The median full-time salary in 2025 was €54,066 gross, and only about a third of employees earn more than the average. A comparison with averages therefore refers to a figure that is pulled upwards by a few very large fortunes.

bloecke.unter: Average gross financial assets per household, excluding property and before deducting debts; due to rounding, the parts add up to €74,800.

Classify each item as fixed or variable, depending on how long it takes before it can be changed. Divide annual payments by twelve.
Net income minus expenditure, divided by net income. Note down the definition you have chosen (with or without repayments).

schritte.titel: Draw up a balance sheet for a reference date
schritte.text: Balances and assets on one side, debts on the other. A sheet of paper is enough as long as the date is noted.

schritte.titel: Set up a standing order and review it after three months
schritte.text: Schedule the savings amount for the day after your salary arrives. If the account then regularly runs short, the amount was too high. That only shows it needs adjusting.

bloecke.md:
With **zero-based budgeting**, every euro is given a job in advance until nothing is left over. It is the most precise and at the same time the most laborious method, and it pays off above all when money is tight or debts are being paid down.

The **envelope method** divides cash into envelopes for each category. Its effect rests almost entirely on the fact that cash visibly dwindles. An empty envelope can be seen; an exhausted card limit cannot. With card payments, this effect is therefore lost.

The **reverse budget** does without categories. A fixed savings amount goes out by standing order, and the rest can be spent freely. It is the crudest method and in practice the easiest to keep up for a long time, because it requires no daily decisions.

Five minutes a month for the account balances is enough, plus one hour a year for the balance sheet, the savings rate and the list of fixed costs. More frequent checks do not lead to better decisions; they only create more opportunities to decide wrongly on bad days.

mitnehmen: Income and expenditure are flows over a period, net worth is a stock on a reference date, and only this separation makes both figures useful.
Fixed costs are expenses that cannot be changed in the short term; a one-off cut takes effect twelve times a year.
There is no universally valid definition of the savings rate, so your own rule should stay the same over the years.
On the asset side, what counts is the value realisable today: the surrender value rather than the premiums paid in, and the selling price rather than the price when new.
Averages are not a suitable benchmark for wealth and salaries; for wealth, the median is less than half the mean, and for salaries the gap is smaller.

begriffe.text: A quantity that refers to a period, such as income or expenditure per month. Its counterpart is the stock variable, which applies to a reference date, for example wealth.

Expenses that cannot be changed in the short term because they are tied to contracts, notice periods or laws. Regular expenses are not automatically fixed costs: groceries arise every month but can be influenced immediately.
The percentage of net income that is not spent. There is no generally binding definition. Whether loan repayments and retirement contributions count is up to you, and you then stick with that choice.
The sum of all assets on a reference date less all debts. Realisable values are used, not purchase prices or amounts paid in.

The amount a life or pension insurance policy pays out on early surrender. In the first years of the contract it is usually below the total premiums paid in, because acquisition and distribution costs are offset up front.
